title: Spotting Psychology Myths
objective: After this level you can weigh popular claims, like learning styles and venting anger, against the research evidence.
summary: Two popular claims, tested: matching teaching to 'learning styles' has virtually no evidence behind it, and venting anger tends to feed it rather than drain it.

cards.headline: "I'm a visual learner." "Let it out, you'll feel better."
cards.body: Both sound like common sense, and both come with a theory. Learning styles says teaching should match how you like to learn. Venting says anger drains away once you release it. Here's what happened when researchers tested them.

cards.headline: Learning styles: preference isn't proof
cards.body: The learning-styles idea says you learn best when teaching matches your preferred mode, like pictures for a "visual learner". It's widespread in education, from kindergarten to graduate school. And people do have preferences: ask, and almost anyone will name one. But liking a format and learning better from it are two different claims.

cards.headline: What the evidence showed
cards.body: In 2008 Harold Pashler and colleagues reviewed the research. They found plenty of evidence that people state preferences, but virtually no evidence that matching teaching to them improves learning. Some well-designed studies flatly contradicted it. Their advice: spend limited education budgets on practices with strong evidence instead.

cards.headline: Venting feeds the flame
cards.body: The idea of venting goes back to Josef Breuer and Sigmund Freud, who held that expressing pent-up emotion beats bottling it up: anger as pressure that needs a release valve. In 2002 Brad Bushman tested it. Angered people who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who angered them felt angrier and acted more aggressively than people who did nothing. Doing nothing beat venting.

mascot.line: It connects: this is Level 4's Freud again, and again the tested details didn't hold.

cards.headline: Myths, tested
learned: People state learning preferences, but matching doesn't help
Spend on teaching methods with strong evidence
Venting anger tends to feed it
Popular claims get weighed by what the experiments found

questions.prompt: In Brad Bushman's 2002 study, how did people who hit a punching bag while thinking about their provoker end up?

options.label: Calmer than the people who did nothing at all
options.rationale: Doing nothing worked better than venting.

options.label: Exactly as angry as they were before hitting
options.rationale: Their anger went up, not flat.

options.label: Angrier and more aggressive than the do-nothing group
Too tired to feel much anger at all
options.rationale: The study measured more anger and aggression.

questions.explanation: Venting while dwelling on the provoker increased anger and aggression; doing nothing worked better.

questions.prompt: A school plans to test every student's learning style and teach each one in that style. What does the research suggest?

options.label: It will sharply raise every student's grades
options.rationale: There's virtually no evidence that matching helps.

options.label: Little evidence it helps; fund proven methods instead
It works, but only for visual learners
Students don't have any preferences at all
options.rationale: They do state preferences; matching them just doesn't help.

questions.explanation: Pashler's review found virtually no evidence that matching teaching to learning styles improves learning.

questions.prompt: The idea that venting drains pent-up anger traces back partly to which thinker from Level 4?

options.label: Wilhelm Wundt
options.rationale: Wundt measured reaction times in his lab.

questions.explanation: Breuer and Freud held that expressing pent-up emotion was better than bottling it up, the root of the venting idea.
